content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a new challenge of Continual Learning (CL) called Continual Model Evolvement (CME). The paper argues that compared to traditional continual learning settings that focus on OOD or no-revisiting input stream, CME focuses on the continual learning problem that the task definition itself also changes, such as the question-answering model facing novel answerability problems.

Since CME is more challenging than OOD CL, the paper proposes a new CL method called inner-product restriction, where the model parameters are only updated where its gradients w.r.t the upstream and CL are in the same direction (both positive or negative). Therefore, with the first-term approximation of Taylor expansion, the CL process will not hurt the upstream performance.

Experimental results on CME/OOD-QA show that combining with experience replay methods (for upstream loss calculation), inner-product restriction (IP) achieves significantly better performance than pure experience replay (ER) method or ER + L2-regularization methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

1. While most previous work on CL focuses on continual learning on OOD data, such as Split CIFAR-100. This paper proposes a new and reasonable paradigm for continual learning, i.e., fine-tuning a QA model into a QA + answerability model. Such a Continual Model Evolvement (CME) scheme is novel and interesting to my knowledge.

2. The paper proposes a novel CL technique (IP) where the model parameters are only updated where its gradients w.r.t the upstream and CL are in the same direction. Experimental results show that IP, especially IP-Optim. can significantly improve the CL model performance.

Weaknesses

1. Besides the QA => answerability task, could the authors point out a few other potential tasks that fall into the CME category? Otherwise, the proposed Continual Model Evolvement term just looks like a more fancy term to describe QA => answerability task to me.

2. For now, all the experiments on based on the new CME/OOD-QA. Since IP shows as a strong CL method combined with ER, I believe more experiments of IP on traditional CL datasets such as CIFAR and comparison to state-of-the-art CL techniques can further improve the quality of the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written and technically correct. It proposes a novel CL scheme and a novel CL method.

However, since all the results in the paper are only based on their proposed new dataset CME/OOD-QA, open-sourced code and implementation are necessary for reproducing and follow-up work.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a novel and interesting CL scheme and a novel CL method and demonstrates quite strong experimental reports. Though, one problem is that IP is only evaluated on the new CME/OOD-QA dataset proposed in this paper. Therefore, I recommend the weak acceptance of the paper.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work follows the Continual Model Refinement (CMR) setting in Lin et al . (2022) to formulate a more challenging problem, named Continual Model Evolvement (CME), for the question-answering task. Unlike CMR, which merely considers out-of-distribution samples, CME explores both unanswerable questions and out-of-distribution samples. This paper also borrows most of the baselines and metrics in CMR to test their performance in the newly presented CME setting. Besides, they also propose an inner-product Regularization strategy and the correlated optimization method. Experiments on the question-answering task demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.



[1] On Continual Model Refinement in Out-of-Distribution Data Streams
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
1. This paper explores a more realistic setting of the question-answering task, which specifies the out-of-distribution (OOD) samples in the CMR (Lin et al.) setting with two different categories, i.e., evolved unanswerable samples and OOD samples.
2. Studies on existing continual learning methods demonstrate the proposed problem formulation (like CMR) is also an open challenge.

Weaknesses: 
1. This work only explores the question-answering task, which cannot adequately prove that CME is an open challenge for existing CL methods.

2. It is also difficult to conclude that CME is more challenging than the existing setting, e.g., compared with CMR. It can be seen from the left upper part of Table 1 that exiting CL methods can achieve (at least) comparable EKR/EKG scores with OKR/OKG. In other words, the evolving answerable samples are not more difficult than OOD samples constructed in the previous CMR setting.

3. Besides, the newly introduced methods can not achieve a consistent improvement over existing methods.

4. More experiments and results are required. For instance, it would be better to explore and report the training efficiency (convergence speed) with/without the newly introduced strategies. 

5. Part of the results or descriptions are Problematic, e.g., ``Offline Fine-Tuning'' is considered as the upper bound but with a lower UKR^(T) score than the ``Frozen'' baseline.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is generally well-written. The formulated new problem is meaningful for the question-answering task.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper follows the previous continual model refinement (CMR) setting to formulate another problem, i.e., continual model evolvement (CME), with fine-grained challenging samples (both evolving samples and OOD data) expect for out-of-distribution samples. A training strategy is presented but fails to achieve consistent performance improvement.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper formulates and focuses on the continual model evolvement (CME) problem, which is a relatively hard setting in the continual learning problem of pretrained models. In the CME setting, the model needs to address incoming challenging inputs while not forgetting the abilities learned from the upstream data – a typical continual learning description. Specifically, this paper uses question answering tasks as the testbed and the incoming samples consist of unanswerable questions and OOD questions. The authors first evaluate standard CL baselines such as experience replay and L2 regularization, then propose new methods based on the inner product between the gradients of new samples and upstream samples to mitigate the catastrophic forgetting issue. The proposed method is not very empirically advantageous over the baselines in my view (see details below)
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths:

1. The problem of focus is important – the evolvement/updates of LLMs is a critical direction to pursue given the huge cost of training LLMs  
2. The proposed inner product approach is novel.


### Weaknesses:

1. I think the paper writing (e.g. the title, abstract, and intro) overclaims the actual experiments in the paper – the paper tries to tell a **general** model evolvement story while only testing the methods on a question answering task with (mainly) one pair of QA datasets. The discussion on unanswerable questions in the CME formulation is also unique to QA tasks. I don’t think QA tasks are general or representative enough (even though they are, one pair of QA datasets is definitely not general enough) for such a story – any conclusion in this paper may not generalize to other tasks or models. Either multiple seq2seq tasks or language modeling task is representative in my view. Therefore, I think this paper is more like “continual model evolvement for question answering” and the writing across the entire paper (including the title, abstract, intro, etc.) should be revised accordingly.  
2. This paper explains a lot about the CME formulation and views it as one of the main contributions. However, I don’t feel it is that different from the traditional CL setup from the experiments, it is more like a relatively hard example of CL from my perspective.  
3. The proposed inner product approach does not outperform traditional CL methods like experience replay. When I compare the EFR, UKR, EKR, EKG, OKR, OKG metrics, no IR variants outperform ER (k=1) on all metrics. Actually, I feel ER strikes a good balance among the five metrics.

### Other Questions/Suggestions:
1. Please cite references with brackets when it is not part of the grammar, e.g. HotPotQA (Yang et al. 2018)  
2. Eq. (1), I don’t think $L_{ft}(\theta) = L_{ft}(\theta - \eta\Delta L_{cl}(\theta))$ is correct  
3. The appendix mentioned the penalty weight of L2-regularization is set as 1 in all experiments. Why is that? Shouldn’t it be tuned on some validation set? I feel such an arbitrary setup of hyperparameters would hurt the baseline a lot.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed method is novel, the writing is clear, but the quality is not very high from my perspective (see weaknesses above)
content.summary_of_the_review: I don’t recommend acceptance of this paper because 1. Its writing overstates the actual experiments in the paper, and 2. The results of the proposed method are not clearly advantageous over the baselines
